  Nivolumab's exposure–response is flat, and that flatness carried three
  regimen changes into the label. It is also the single easiest result in
  clinical pharmacology to over-read — and the analysis that produces it is
  observational, whatever the trial around it was.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## The decision this serves
Your exposure–response analysis comes back flat. The clinical pharmacology lead
reads it as permission to double the interval. The medical director, in the same
meeting, reads it as permission to halve the **dose** — same drug, half the cost,
and the curve says exposure does not matter.

One of them is right, and the analysis on the slide cannot tell you which. This
lesson is about what a flat line permits, and about the more uncomfortable
question of whether the line you fitted was measuring exposure at all.
:::

## 1. What was actually approved

Nivolumab was licensed in December 2014 at **3 mg/kg every two weeks**
([BLA 125554](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cder/daf/index.cfm?event=overview.process&ApplNo=125554),
Bristol Myers Squibb). Since then the regimen has moved twice: to a flat
**240 mg Q2W**, and then to **480 mg every four weeks**.

Check the label today and the arc is complete. On the version effective
31 August 2026, adult monotherapy dosing is *240 mg every 2 weeks or 480 mg
every 4 weeks*; the weight-based 3 mg/kg regimen the drug was approved on
survives only for paediatric patients under 40 kg. The dose that carried the
original evidence is no longer the dose adults receive.

None of those changes was supported by a new efficacy trial. All of them rested
on the same finding: over the exposure range the programme produced, outcome did
not vary with exposure.

## 2. What "flat" meant, exactly

It is worth quoting the shape of the claim rather than the slogan, because the
slogan is wrong.

The adjuvant analysis is Zhao et al.
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1111/bcp.16188)): a population PK model on **1,493
subjects** across seven monotherapy studies, and an exposure–response analysis on
**756 patients** from CheckMate 577. Nivolumab exposure *was* associated with
disease-free survival, and *was* associated with grade ≥2 immune-mediated adverse
events. What the authors report as flat is that the hazard ratios at the 5th and
95th percentiles of exposure were **similar to each other** — the association
exists, but across the whole span of exposures the regimen actually produced, it
does not move the outcome enough to matter.

"Flat" is therefore not "exposure is irrelevant". It is "over *this* range, the
slope is small enough to ignore". Those are different sentences and only the
second one is licensed.

The regimen comparison is Long et al.
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1093/annonc/mdy408)): 480 mg Q4W against 3 mg/kg Q2W
gives a similar time-averaged concentration, an approximately **16% lower
trough**, and an approximately **45% higher peak** — with that peak still well
below 10 mg/kg Q2W, a dose already tolerated. The same three-legged argument as
[C-02](../c-02-a-regimen-without-a-trial/index.qmd), with flatness doing the work
that pembrolizumab's exposure–response curve did there.

## 3. Flatness is the expected answer, not a discovery

Here is the part that rarely gets said in the slide deck. A phase 3 programme
studies **one dose**. The exposure range in an exposure–response analysis
therefore comes not from design but from between-subject variability in
pharmacokinetics — a spread of maybe three- to fourfold, sitting wherever the
chosen dose put it.

If that dose was selected, as these were, at or above the top of the
dose–response curve, then every patient in the analysis is on the plateau, and a
flat line is what a plateau looks like when you sample it. The analysis has
confirmed that the dose is not *too low*. It has said nothing whatsoever about
whether it is too high, because no one in the dataset received less.

That asymmetry is the whole answer to the meeting in the callout above. Flatness
licenses **redistributing** the same exposure over a different schedule. It does
not license **reducing** it, because the region below the studied range is not in
the data. Answering the medical director's question requires a randomised
lower-dose arm, which is exactly what Project Optimus now asks for and what [`C-04`](../../drugs.qmd)
will be about.

## 4. The confound

Now the harder problem, and the reason this lesson exists rather than being a
paragraph in C-02.

Nivolumab's clearance is **time-varying** — Bajaj et al.
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12143)), a population model on 1,895 patients
across eleven trials, describes linear pharmacokinetics with a clearance that
falls over the course of treatment. Clearance of a monoclonal antibody reflects
catabolic activity, and catabolic activity is elevated in advanced cancer. When a
patient responds, their clearance drops.

So exposure is not an exogenous variable. It is partly a **measurement of how
sick the patient is**, taken with a pharmacokinetic instrument.

Turner et al. ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-18-0415)) put numbers
on this for pembrolizumab across 1,453 subjects. Overall survival was
dose-independent from 2 to 10 mg/kg — hazard ratio 0.98 (95% CI 0.94–1.02) in
melanoma and 0.98 (0.95–1.01) in NSCLC. But baseline clearance predicted survival
powerfully: unadjusted hazard ratios of **2.56 (1.72–3.80)** and **2.64
(1.94–3.57)**. High clearance tracked the markers of cancer anorexia–cachexia
syndrome. The paper's own conclusion is that this pattern is probably general to
antineoplastic monoclonal antibodies, not specific to one drug.

The cleanest evidence is a natural experiment. Hamuro et al.
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.1502)) looked at nivolumab in patients whose
melanoma had been **surgically removed**. In that population clearance was 40%
lower at baseline and **did not vary with time at all**. Remove the tumour and
the time-varying clearance disappears with it — which is about as direct a
demonstration as observational pharmacokinetics ever gets that the clearance was
a property of the disease rather than of the drug.

## 5. Adjusting for prognosis does not rescue it

The instinctive fix is to put the prognostic covariates in the model. Turner et
al. did. The clearance–survival association was attenuated and **did not go
away**: multivariate-adjusted hazard ratios of 1.64 (1.06–2.52) in melanoma and
1.88 (1.22–2.89) in NSCLC.

This is not a failure of diligence. The covariates recorded on a case report form
are noisy readings of the underlying disease burden, and adjusting for a noisy
proxy removes only the fraction of the confounding the proxy managed to capture.
The residual is invisible and points in a known direction: it makes low exposure
look worse than it is.

## 6. The diagnostic that works

Stop comparing high exposure against low exposure inside the treated arm. That
comparison is observational no matter how randomised the trial was — the protocol
assigned the **dose**; the patient's physiology assigned the **exposure**.

Ask a different question instead: do the patients in the *lowest* exposure
quartile still beat comparable patients who never received the drug? If they do,
the exposure gradient was never a gradient in drug effect.

He et al. ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.3063)) ran exactly this on
tremelimumab in the phase 3 POSEIDON study. Higher exposure looked associated
with better progression-free and overall survival. Case-matching the lowest
exposure quartile against comparable chemotherapy-treated patients returned
hazard ratios of **1.04 (0.76–1.44)** for overall survival and **0.99
(0.72–1.36)** for progression-free survival — and the authors concluded the
apparent exposure–response "might be confounded".

## Work through it

The notebook builds a trial in which exposure has *exactly* no effect on outcome,
runs the analysis anyone would run, and watches it report a 67% hazard reduction
with a confidence interval nowhere near 1. It then applies covariate adjustment
(which removes about half the bias) and case-matching (which removes most of it),
and finishes with the sabotage run that proves where the bias came from.

## Failure mode — the flat line that was never tested

Two ways this goes wrong, and neither of them errors.

**Flatness assumed rather than shown.** A team reports a flat exposure–response
and moves to a longer interval. Nobody asks what fraction of the exposure range
the analysis actually covered, and it turns out the interquartile range spans
1.4-fold. A relationship can be arbitrarily steep and still look flat across
1.4-fold of anything. The analysis had no power to detect the slope it is being
used to rule out — and a confidence interval on the slope would have said so,
which is why the slope interval, not the p-value, is the number to demand.

**The confounded slope read backwards.** The opposite failure, and the more
expensive one. A team finds a *positive* exposure–response — more drug, better
survival — and proposes raising the dose. What they have found is that patients
who were going to do well cleared the antibody slowly. Raising the dose treats a
symptom of good prognosis as its cause. Everyone gets more drug, more toxicity,
and no benefit, and the trial that discovers this costs years.

The diagnostic for both is the same and it is not a diagnostic plot: it is
asking what would have to be true of the world for this coefficient to be causal,
and then checking that thing directly.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## The habit
Before you present an exposure–response result from a single-arm-of-a-trial
analysis, write down the mechanism by which a patient came to have high exposure.
If any part of that mechanism is "they were doing well", the coefficient is not
a dose effect and no amount of covariate adjustment will make it one.
:::

## Check yourself

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Your exposure–response is flat, and someone proposes cutting the dose in half. What is wrong with the argument, and what would fix it?

The flat line was fitted over the exposure range one dose produced. Half that
dose lands outside it, where the analysis has no data and therefore no opinion —
flatness there is an extrapolation, not a finding. Nothing about the existing
analysis can be re-run to fix this; it needs exposure at the lower level, which
in practice means a randomised lower-dose arm. Note that the same flat line
*does* support redistributing the same total exposure over a longer interval,
because that stays inside the observed range. Same result, two proposals, only
one of them supported.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. A colleague shows that patients in the top exposure quartile survive far longer than those in the bottom quartile, and concludes the dose should go up. What is the first thing you ask for?

The baseline characteristics of the two quartiles. If the drug is a monoclonal
antibody, expect the low-exposure group to have higher tumour burden, lower
albumin, worse performance status and higher LDH — because clearance rises with
catabolic burden, so sorting by exposure sorts by prognosis. The second thing to
ask for is the case-matched comparison against a control arm: whether the
*lowest*-exposure patients still beat comparable untreated patients. If they do,
the gradient is confounding. Adjusting for the baseline covariates is worth
doing but will not settle it, since it removes only the part of the confounding
those covariates measured.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Nivolumab clearance falls over time in metastatic melanoma but is constant in resected melanoma. Why does that observation matter more than a covariate analysis?

Because it is a difference in the *system*, not a coefficient inside one model.
A covariate analysis can always be argued about — was the right covariate
included, was it measured well, was the functional form right. Removing the
tumour and watching the time dependence vanish with it identifies what the
clearance was tracking, without needing a model to be correctly specified. It is
the closest thing to an intervention available here, and it converts "clearance
correlates with disease" into "clearance is a reading of disease".
:::

## Going further

Zhao Y, Tsujimoto A, Ide T, et al. *Model-based population pharmacokinetic and
exposure response analyses for safety and efficacy of nivolumab as adjuvant
treatment in subjects with resected oesophageal or gastroesophageal junction
cancer.* Br J Clin Pharmacol 2024;90:2920–2930
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1111/bcp.16188)) — the flat-E-R analysis behind the
adjuvant Q4W regimen.

Turner DC, Kondic AG, Anderson KM, et al. *Pembrolizumab exposure-response
assessments challenged by association of cancer cachexia and catabolic
clearance.* Clin Cancer Res 2018;24:5841–5849
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-18-0415)) — the paper to read if you
read only one. Note the title: the authors are not claiming the confounding is
hypothetical.

Hamuro L, Statkevich P, Bello A, Roy A, Bajaj G. *Nivolumab clearance is
stationary in patients with resected melanoma on adjuvant therapy: implications
of disease status on time-varying clearance.* Clin Pharmacol Ther
2019;106:1018–1027 ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.1502)).

He JZ, Duval V, Jauslin P, et al. *Population pharmacokinetics and
exposure-response analysis for the CTLA-4 inhibitor tremelimumab in metastatic
NSCLC patients in the phase III POSEIDON study.* Clin Pharmacol Ther
2023;114:1375–1386 ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.3063)) — the case-matching
diagnostic, done in public on a registrational dataset.

Bajaj G, Wang X, Agrawal S, Gupta M, Roy A, Feng Y. *Model-based population
pharmacokinetic analysis of nivolumab in patients with solid tumors.* CPT
Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol 2017;6:58–66
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12143), free full text).

Long GV, Tykodi SS, Schneider JG, et al. *Assessment of nivolumab exposure and
clinical safety of 480 mg every 4 weeks flat-dosing schedule in patients with
cancer.* Ann Oncol 2018;29:2208–2213
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1093/annonc/mdy408), free full text).

**What this lesson deliberately omits.** The formal causal machinery — marginal
structural models, g-estimation, instrumental variables — that the pharmacometric
literature is beginning to import for exactly this problem. The point here is to
make the confounding visible and to show one diagnostic that works on data you
already have. Doing it properly is a course of its own.

All citations verified against **PubMed**; DOIs link to the publisher record.
